When I moved from Sydney to Houston, I thought English was the easy part. English is my first language, right? Well, on my first day, I asked for a glass of water in a restaurant, and the waiter just looked at me. I didn't pronounce the r, and he didn't understand. It happened again and again. People were friendly, but I wasn't used to their accent, and they weren't used to mine. I felt a bit shy for the first time in my life. Now, after three years, I'm used to the Texas accent, and my colleagues are used to me. So every accent is just practice, even for native speakers.

I work in a law firm in Berlin, and we have clients in many countries. For years, I used to stay silent in international meetings. I understood everything, but I only took notes. I was afraid of making mistakes, with my accent and with my grammar. Then a partner told me something simple: nobody remembers your mistakes, but they remember if you never speak. So I tried two things. First, I prepare one question before every meeting. Second, I speak in the first ten minutes, before I get nervous. It wasn't easy at the start, but now I'm used to it, and I feel much more confident.

I'm from India, and I've worked as a tour guide in Kyoto for five years. When I arrived, I spoke English every day, but English in Japan was difficult for me. The rhythm was different, and some sounds changed. For example, many people added a small vowel at the end of words. At first, when I didn't understand, I used to smile and say yes. That was a mistake. Now I'm used to it. I ask people to repeat, and I listen to the rhythm and the important words, not every sound. I always tell tourists the same thing: it's normal to ask again. People are happy to help you.
